Container freight rates: Transpacific strength offsets European weakness

Container freight rates have remained broadly rangebound since July, when the Drewry World Container Index reached a two-year high of USD 4,638 per 40-foot container. This week’s reading of USD 4,389 masks significant regional divergences. Over the past four months, the index has declined around 5%, with sharp falls of 27% and 36% on routes to Rotterdam and Genoa partly offset by increases of 17% on routes to Los Angeles and New York.

The divergence reflects differences in demand, shipping capacity and geopolitical exposure. US-bound rates have benefited from trade policy uncertainty, front-loaded imports and shipping disruptions, while European routes face weaker demand and growing capacity availability. Expectations of a gradual reopening of shorter Middle East shipping routes have added pressure on European rates, highlighting how regional developments can differ substantially from the broader global benchmark.

EIAs latest inventory report: US crude oil and fuel inventories all declined last week, with modest draws in crude and gasoline overshadowed by a 3.6 mb drop in distillate stocks, pushing the total below 100 million barrels for the first time since 2003.

Crude production reached a fresh record above 14 mb/d having fully recovered from a recent weather related slump, while SPR withdrawals slowed to just 400 kb/d. Crude exports fell by 1.2 mb/d to below 4 mb/d, while gasoline and distillate exports both increased. Meanwhile, crude imports from Canada approached 4 mb/d, contributing to an inventory build at Cushing, with the Midwest remaining the largest US destination for Canadian crude.

Refinery crude runs remained at a seasonal record of 16.7 mb/d, supported by elevated refining margins and the restart of several facilities following maintenance, particularly across the Midwest and Gulf Coast.

Crude oil tumbled 8% on Wednesday. 
It is probably no coincidence that the front-month Brent contract has slumped by more than 16% this week, with roughly half of that decline occurring following the US midterm election results. President Trump has acknowledged that Republican losses were largely linked to the Iran conflict and rising fuel prices, while signalling no immediate escalation of military strikes.  He appears increasingly keen to move on from the conflict, while Iran may have achieved one of its political objectives by contributing to a Republican defeat through elevated energy prices. A Democratic-controlled Congress could also increase pressure on Washington to bring the war to an end.

Attention now turns to negotiations and whether a credible agreement can be reached. The oil market is clearly pricing in an increased likelihood of a diplomatic breakthrough, but no deal has been reached, and the two sides could still be far apart. To sustain the recent decline in prices, the market needs to see positive signals from both Tehran and Washington pointing to genuine progress and a willingness to compromise. So far, the sharp selloff has been driven more by hopes of a breakthrough than by concrete announcements or tangible progress towards an agreement. Without such progress, prices could quickly rebound as traders reassess the risk of prolonged supply disruptions.
